body_markdown:
We are constantly monitoring the collector car and truck market at Hagerty, noting the subtle fluctuations that reflect the whims and preferences of buyers across the country. Whether it’s the result of pop culture sentiment or changing demographics, we track the numbers and update our price guide quarterly to maintain fresh data on classic truck values. Our newest update shows things are rather stable in the collector truck and 4×4 market, with most models we track remaining steady. But they’re not all stable, and here are the six biggest movers in the segment: three that moved up slightly and three that dropped, each based on their condition #2 (excellent) values.


## [1921–27 Ford Model T Roadster Pickup](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/model_t/1927/1927-ford-model_t-base?id=aCn1I000000CsfQSAS)


Josh Sweeney


**Average #2 Value: $20,800 (+7.8%)**


Ford’s Model T was *the* car of the 1910s and 1920s. Famous for its mass production and affordability that democratized personal motorized transportation, it was built in the millions. From its first iteration in 1908 until the final versions that were built before the 1928 Model A replaced it, the Model T went through a constant evolution, so much so that a pair produced on either end of the 20-year production run would hardly be identifiable as the same car.


There’s a wide gulf in values in Model Ts, divided between body style as well as between those in #1 (concours) or #2 (excellent) condition and those in #3 (dood) or #4 (fair) condition. The trend applies to both early and late production. We’ve noted price increases in several Model T variants, but it’s the drop-top pickups that have seen the largest gains and remain significantly more valuable than many of their closed-cabin counterparts, possibly because few managed to save these early workhorses.


## [1960–66 Chevrolet C/K](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/k10/1966/1966-chevrolet-k10-1!!2_ton?id=aCn1I000000DI7mSAG)


Hagerty Marketplace


**Average #2 value: $39,600 (+4%)**


Chevrolet’s first-generation C/K pickup falls between the fabulous ‘50s styling of its “Task Force” predecessors and the elegant yet muscular look of the 1967–72 “Action Line” that followed. Bookended with such notable collectibles that are also prized by hotrodders and customizers, these ‘60s haulers have also managed to become a collector favorite, especially in the last 10 to15 years. Lately, condition #1 values have eclipsed those of its successor.


After its initial, polarizing design was tamed by a new hood in 1962, Chevrolet further updated the C/K truck line in 1964 with a redesigned cab that ditched the wraparound windshield. Most were powered by Chevrolet’s venerable inline-six engines in 235, 250, and 292-cubic-inch displacements. The optional 283 V-8s demand a premium, as does Chevrolet’s vaunted 327 V-8, which finally trickled down to ½-ton models in 1966. The most prized combination is a V-8 Fleetside, with 4×4 models commanding a 20-40% premium over their 2WD counterparts.


## [1959–71 Land Rover Series II-IIA](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/land_rover/series_iia_88/1970/1970-land_rover-series_iia_88-base?id=aCn1I000000D9QcSAK)


Land Rover


**Average #2 Value: $46,000 (+2%)**


Land Rover’s spartan and rugged Series I 4x4s got some significant updates to kick off the Series II production in 1958. Most noticeable is the wider track and correspondingly wider body. The previously flat door skins were replaced by skins that kick out 2+ inches per side that are matched by fenders (wings) and quarter panels with a matching width that all blend into the body with a generous radius.


These beloved off-roaders have dropped in value over the past year, so this 2% climb marks a small upward correction, but they’re still down year-over-year. As with many of its 4×4 counterparts, buyers put a premium on soft-tops and prefer the more powerful gasoline powertrain over its diesel counterpart.


## [1955–59 Chevrolet Trucks](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/series_3100/1958/1958-chevrolet-series_3100-1!!2_ton?id=aCn1I000000DDxCSAW)


collectibleclassics/Hagerty Marketplace


**Average #2 Value: $51,900 (-3%)**


Chevrolet’s popular line of pickups had a lot in common with its passenger car counterparts in the ’50s. They were based on the same basic chassis design and mirrored the styling changes that came each year. Note the similarities between a[1955 Bel Air](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1955+chevrolet+bel+air) and a 1955 pickup, for example. When Chevy adapted the hood spears of the[1955 Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1955+chevrolet+corvette) to the passenger car line in ’57, the pickups got them as well. Of course, when quad headlights became a styling option for Detroit cars in 1958, pickups joined in on that styling trend too.


You might be surprised to learn that the beautiful and rare Cameo pickups—which were available from 1955 to1957 and featured fiberglass bedsides that forecast the widespread adoption of fleetside styling—are not the most expensive variant of this generation. Both 1958-1959 Suburbans and pickups fitted with a factory 4×4 drivetrain, as well as 1955–57 pickups fitted with 4×4 conversion from NAPCO, remain the collector favorites of this generation. This slight correction in price eliminates a small gains earlier this year.


## [1942–45 Willys MB and Ford GPW](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/gpw/1943/1943-ford-gpw-1!!4_ton?id=aCn1I000000DDSVSA4)


Amy Shore


**Average #2 Value: $32,900 (-5.1%)**


The original Jeep as we know it helped win WWII for the Allies and led to the first successful commercial 4x4s in America. The compact, simple, tough Jeep served as the inspiration for numerous off-roaders around the globe, including the aforementioned Land Rover. The current Wrangler proudly retains plenty of the original Jeep’s DNA with its overall shape, seven-slot grille (thanks Ford), and folding windshield all evolving from the 1940s original.


We’re not noticing any major trends with values here. This small drop in price leaves Willys and Ford WWII Jeeps almost exactly where they were a year ago.


## [1966–77 Ford Bronco](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/bronco/1971/1971-ford-bronco-base?id=aCn1I000000D4idSAC)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


**Average #2 Value: $53,700 (-14%)**


Ford’s first foray into consumer SUVs, the compact and stylish Bronco led the charge in collector demand for vintage 4x4s in the 2010s and early 2020s, bringing Blazers, Jimmys, and all manner of Jeeps along for the ride. Whether it’s a well-worn original complete with patina, a[restomod sporting a rowdy, modern V8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/velocity-modern-classics-modernized-bronco-is-still-wild-at-heart/) , or[an amalgam of both](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/icons-first-derelict-bronco-is-burnished-to-perfection/) , Broncos have remained popular in just about every format.


The 14% drop in value recorded in the latest valuation marks two straight drops for Bronco, which is down significantly across #1, #2, and #3 valuations and about where it was in 2019. The #4 Broncos are the only ones still holding their value over the past year. Even as the high end of the Bronco is slowing down, perhaps due to competition from other high-end resotmods, it seems buyers still enjoy a project they can invest a little bit of money in and enjoy as a driver.


The post[Six Classic Truck Values That Moved the Most This Summer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/six-classic-truck-values-that-moved-the-most-this-summer/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
